lines: Two separate dashboards, built from the exact same underlying mart, report two different totals for the same question.
Both engineers look at their own query and genuinely believe it's correct, because, taken on its own, it actually is.
So how can two correct queries land on two different answers.
Here's the real question underneath that contradiction.
What fact was simply never written down anywhere that would have kept this from happening in the first place.
And whose responsibility should writing that fact down have actually been.
answer: Neither engineer made a mistake in their own SQL at all.
What nobody ever documented was what one single row of that mart actually represents, so one query ended up counting at a finer level of detail than the other without anyone intending it.

lines: Here is exactly what crosses that boundary, and nothing more.
A properly conformed table, sitting behind a layer that turns one shared metric definition into the right query for whichever tool is asking.
Never a raw, unprocessed table on its own, and never a finished dashboard either.
Two specific facts have to travel across that boundary in writing, not just in someone's head.
First, exactly what one row of that table actually represents. Second, exactly how stale that table is allowed to get before it's considered a problem.
Leave either one unspoken, and it quietly turns into an assumption, which then breaks the very first time it actually matters.
Past this exact point, who typically ends up owning a metric's definition changes.
It becomes the analytics engineers' job, not the job of the data engineers who built the underlying table in the first place.
Moving enormous amounts of data around reliably and correctly defining a business metric turn out to be two genuinely different skills.
So what actually keeps a shared metric from quietly being computed two different ways by two different people.
It's deciding, out loud, who's even allowed to change a shared definition, and exactly how a disagreement about it gets resolved when it comes up.
That decision-making never finishes. It's a living process, not a document someone wrote once and then filed away.
A real company built exactly this, at a genuinely large scale.
Their own internal metrics platform was built specifically so that metrics get created, computed, served, and consumed all through one single, standardized path.
Every metric lives in exactly one place, computed on their workflow and processing tools, and served out through their own serving layer underneath.
A few things on purpose don't get covered here.
How that shared layer actually compiles a definition down into real queries was already covered earlier in this course.
Which specific tool an analyst actually opens, the engine that keeps many tools fast at once, and the full back-and-forth of negotiating a definition, each get covered properly later on instead.
Bringing the whole thing together now.
A conformed table and one compiled metric definition are what actually cross this boundary. Grain and freshness get written down explicitly, never left to be guessed at.
Ownership of the metric itself shifts over to analytics engineers. And an ongoing negotiation, not a one-time document, is what actually keeps that metric computed only once.
A third dashboard shows up, built against that exact same table, and it reports yet another different number for the same metric.
The analyst who built it explains that they simply wrote their own query by hand instead of using the shared definition.
Given everything just covered, what actually broke here, and where exactly did it break.
answer: Nothing broke in the underlying table, and nothing broke in the shared metric layer either, since neither one even changed.
Writing a metric's logic by hand instead of calling the shared definition is, by its very nature, computing that same thing a second, completely independent time.
